scribe_response.text: Tell me about a journey you have never forgotten. The journey I never forget is the train to Whitby in the summer of nineteen fifty-eight. I was ten and Peter was fourteen, and we were um going alone to stay with Auntie Dorothy. My father had arranged a railway pass, so the fare cost us nothing at all. Mother packed a cheese and pickle sandwich each, and two apples. She pinned a label with my name and address to my cardigan, as if I um were a parcel. Peter said it was babyish and took his label off as soon as the platform was behind us. We left Leeds Central on a cold grey Saturday morning with steam hissing under the roof. The carriage had thick green seats that smelled of um dust, and a luggage rack made of netting. A conductor with a bristly moustache punched our tickets and winked at me. I uh pressed my nose to the window and counted every chimney between Leeds and York. Beyond York the fields opened out, green and gold, with cows lying down because rain was coming. Peter read his comic and pretended not to be excited, but his foot never stopped tapping. At Malton a woman got in carrying a basket of eggs and a hen that complained loudly. What happened next? She shared a bag of mint imperials with us and told us about her nine uh grandchildren. Then the train began to climb across the moors, and the world went purple and brown. There were sheep on the line at one point, and the driver let the whistle um go for ages. I remember the smell of heather coming, heather coming through the open window, mixed with coal smoke. Peter finally put his comic down and said it was the best view in England. I was so surprised that he agreed with me that, me that I forgot to be um annoyed. The track followed a river for miles, and herons stood in it like grey umbrellas. Then the line dropped through a tunnel, and we came out into a blaze of light and gulls. I had never seen the sea before, and it looked like a sheet uh of tin with sunshine on it. We pulled into Whitby station at four, and my legs were stiff from sitting so long. Auntie Dorothy was waiting under the clock in a mackintosh and a hat with a feather. She hugged us both so hard that my label came off um and fluttered away. We carried our cases up a hundred and ninety-nine steps to the abbey, because she insisted. Can you tell me more about that? Her house smelled of kippers and lavender polish, and the bed had a quilt of faded squares. That night I listened to the foghorn and the waves and felt uh wonderfully far from home. In the morning we ate fried bread and a kipper each, and I pulled faces. We spent the week on the sand, hunting for fossils and shells and paddling in freezing water. Peter found an ammonite the size of a saucer and carried it everywhere like a trophy. Auntie Dorothy bought, bought us a stick of Whitby rock each. Coming home, I cried um at the station because I did not want the week to end. Peter pretended he had something in his eye, which is how I knew he felt the same. The journey back was quieter, and uh I fell asleep with my head on his shoulder. When we reached Leeds, my father was waiting on the platform in his uniform cap. He lifted me up and swung me round, and I told him I had seen the sea. He said that he knew, because he could smell it on my hair. Whenever I travel now, I think of that little train. It taught me that um going away is a fine way of finding out how much you love home.
